fr:mainmatter.html:p: A set of vectors \{v_1, \dots , v_n\} is called linearly dependent if a_1 v_1 + \dots + a_n v_n = 0 for some a_1, \dots , a_n \in \mathbb {F} with at least one a_i \neq 0 (not all 0).
This note introduces the concept of finite-dimensional vector space. Refer to Linear Algebra Done Right.
Adding up scalar multiples of vectors in a list gives a linear combination.

Let V be a vector space over a field F. Let v_1, \dots , v_n be vectors in V. A linear combination of v_1, \dots , v_n is an expression of the form
a_1 v_1 + \dots + a_n v_n
where a_1, \dots , a_n \in F.
To talk about a structure, we usually define a collection of this structure. Hence we have span for linear combinations.
If \text {span}(v_1, \dots , v_n) = V, we say that v_1, \dots , v_n spans V.

Suppose we have span S=\text {span}(v_1, \dots , v_n). (Span is trivially a subspace.) Obviously for all v_j (1 \leq j \leq n), v_j \in S. Because subspaces are closed under scalar multiplication and addition, every subspace of V containing v_1, \dots , v_n must contain S. Thus we conclude that S is the smallest subspace containing v_1, \dots , v_n.
The discussion about spans leads to a key definition in linear algebra.
A vector space V is called finite-dimensional if some list of vectors v_1, \dots , v_n spans V.
The opposite of finite-dimensional is infinite-dimensional.
A vector space V is called infinite-dimensional if it is not finite-dimensional.

Consider the situation that there is only one way to express a vector v as a linear combination of vectors in a list v_1, \dots , v_n. What property of the list v_1, \dots , v_n does this situation imply? The answer is linear independence.

A set of vectors \{v_1, \dots , v_n\} is called linearly independent if a_1 v_1 + \dots + a_n v_n = 0 implies that a_1 = \dots = a_n = 0. The trivial case of \{0\} is also considered linearly independent.
If some vectors are not linearly independent, then there are more than one way to express a vector as a linear combination of vectors in the list. This leads to the following definition.
A set of vectors \{v_1, \dots , v_n\} is called linearly dependent if a_1 v_1 + \dots + a_n v_n = 0 for some a_1, \dots , a_n \in \mathbb {F} with at least one a_i \neq 0 (not all 0).
The following lemma is a direct consequence of the definition of linear independence. It states that for a given linearly dependent list, we can always remove a vector without changing the span.

Let v_1, \dots , v_n be vectors in a vector space V over a field \mathbb {F}. If v_1, \dots , v_n are linearly dependent, then there exists 1 \leq i \leq n such that
v_i \in \text {span}(v_1, \dots , v_{i-1})
Remove v_i from the list v_1, \dots , v_n and the span does not change

fr:title.text: Length of linearly independent list \leq length of spanning list

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Length of linearly independent list \leq length of spanning list

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In a finite dimensional vector space, the length of a linearly independent list is less than or equal to the length of a spanning list.
We have discussed linear independent lists and spanning lists. Now we are ready to define a basis.
A basis of V is a list of vectors in V that is linearly independent and spans V.
Criterion for basis A list of vectors \{v_1, \dots , v_n\} is a basis of V if and only if every v \in V can be written uniquely as a linear combination of v_1, \dots , v_n.
For instance, we have standard basis \{e_1, \dots , e_n\} for \mathbb {F}^n, where e_i is the vector with 1 at i-th position and 0 elsewhere.
Every spanning list in a vector space can be reduced to a basis.
From the theorem we can infer a corollary.
Every finite-dimensional vector space has a basis.
The next result states for a spanning list can be reduced to a basis. We can adjoin one or more vectors to a linearly independent list to form a basis.

fr:title.text: Linearly dependent list extends to a basis

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Linearly dependent list extends to a basis

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Every linearly independent list of vectors in a finite-dimensional vector space can be extended to a basis.
Recall the definition of direct sum, we can now show that every subspace of a finite-dimensional vector space can be paired with another subspace to form a direct sum of the whole space.

fr:title.text: Direct Sum of Subspaces of V

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Direct Sum of Subspaces of V

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Suppose V is a finite dimensional vector space, and U is a subspace of V. Then there exists a subspace W of V such that V = U \oplus W.

This post discusses about finite-dimensional vector space. But we have not yet defined what is dimension. We tempted to define the dimension as the length of basis intuitively. With this definition we should prove its well-definedness. That is, every basis has the same length.
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space. Then every basis of V has the same length.
This can be proved by Lemma 8. Now we can formally define the dimension of such spaces.
The dimension of a finite-dimensional vector space V is the length of any basis of the vector space. Denoted by \dim V.
Every subspace of a finite-dimensional vector space is also finite-dimensional. Hence we can talk about the dimension of a subspace.
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space, and U be a subspace of V. Then \dim U \leq \dim V.

According to the definition of linearly independent, to show a list of vectors is a basis, we only need to show it is linearly independent, and it spans the whole space. The next theorems simplifies the task:

fr:title.text: Linearly independent list of the right length is a basis

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Linearly independent list of the right length is a basis

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space. Then every linearly independent list of vectors in V with length equal to \dim V is a basis of V.

fr:title.text: Spanning list of the right length is a basis

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Spanning list of the right length is a basis

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space. Then every spanning list of vectors in V with length equal to \dim V is a basis of V.
Now we move to the discussion of the dimension of the sum of two subspaces. This is analogous to the inclusion-exclusion principle.

Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space, and U and W be subspaces of V. Then
\dim (U + W) = \dim U + \dim W - \dim (U \cap W).

fr:title.text: Vector Calculus and Geometry of Space

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Vector Calculus and Geometry of Space

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Notes about multi-variable calculus, geometry of space and linear algebra. Refer to A Visual Introduction to Differential Forms and Calculus on Manifolds.
We now start with introducing the vector space over the field of real numbers \mathbb {R}.

A vector space over a field F is a non-empty set V together with a binary operation and a binary function that satisfy the axioms listed below. In this context, the elements of V are commonly called vectors, and the elements of F are called scalars.
Commutativity: \forall x, y \in V, x + y = y + x
Associativity: \forall x, y, z \in V, (x + y) + z = x + (y + z)
Additive Identity: \exists 0 \in V \text { such that } \forall x \in V, x + 0 = x
Multiplicative Identity: \forall x \in V, 1x = x
Additive Inverse: \forall x \in V, \exists y \in V \text { such that } x + y = 0
Distributivity: \forall x, y \in V, \forall c, d \in F, c(x + y) = cx + cy, (c + d)x = cx + dx
Elements of a vector space are called vectors or points.

Now we will consider a certain type of transformation between vector spaces called a linear transformation. Suppose T is a mapping between \mathbb {R}^n and \mathbb {R}^m, that is T:\mathbb {R}^n\to \mathbb {R}^m, then T is a linear transformation if:
T(c \cdot \vec {v}) = c \cdot T(\vec {v}) \\ T(\vec {v} + \vec {w}) = T(\vec {v}) + T(\vec {w})
If T is a linear transformation from \mathbb {R}^m to \mathbb {R} we simply call it a linear function or a linear functional.

We now turn our attention to the relationship between linear transformation and matrices. We just stick to vector spaces \mathbb {R}^n and the standard basis made up of the Euclidian unit vectors. In order to write linear transformation T:\mathbb {R}^n\to \mathbb {R}^m as a matrix we need ordered bases for both \mathbb {R}^n and \mathbb {R}^m. We can use the intuitively obvious order e_1 < e_2 < \cdots < e_n. Now we can give formal definition of the matrix representation of a linear transformation.

fr:title.text: Matrix Representation of Linear Transformation over \R ^n

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Matrix Representation of Linear Transformation over \R ^n

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
Suppose that T:\mathbb {R}^n\to \mathbb {R}^m is a linear transformation between vector spaces \mathbb {R}^n and \mathbb {R}^m. Let e_1, e_2, \ldots , e_n be the standard basis of \mathbb {R}^n and f_1, f_2, \ldots , f_m be the standard basis of \mathbb {R}^m. Then the matrix representation of T is the m \times n matrix A such that for 1\leq j\leq n:
T(e_j) = \sum _{i=1}^m A_{ij} f_i
where the matrix representation of T is given by the m\times n matrix with entries A_{ij}.

The last major topic in this section is the definition of the dual space. In our discussion, we only concern the dual space of \mathbb {R}^n which is denoted as (\mathbb {R}^n)^*. Now let's consider the dual basis of (\mathbb {R}^n)^* which is denoted as \{T_1, \cdots , T_n\}, which is defined by:
T_i(e_j) = e^i(e_j) = \langle e^i, e_j \rangle = \delta _{j}^i
where \delta _{ij} is the Kronecker delta. We say that T_i is dual to the vector e_i. Note that we also denote T_i as e^i using superscript notation. And the notation \langle e^i, e_j \rangle d indicates the products of row vector e^i and column vector e_j (Usually used in quantum computing).
\alpha (v) = \langle \alpha , v \rangle = [a,b] \times \begin {bmatrix} x \\ y \end {bmatrix} = ax + by
This explains what we always denote elements of the vector space as column vectors, because elements of the dual space are written as row vectors and its very important to distinguish between them.

In linear algebra, dot product or scalar product is an operation that takes two vectors and returns a scalar. Geometrically, it is the product of the Euclidean magnitudes of the two vectors and the cosine of the angle between them. Dot product is also used to define lengths and angles.

The dot product of two vectors \vec {a} = (a_1, a_2, \cdots , a_n) and \vec {b} = (b_1, b_2, \cdots , b_n) is defined as
\vec {a}\cdot \vec {b} = a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + \cdots + a_nb_n = \sum _{i=1}^n a_ib_i.
The dot product is also called the inner product or scalar product. The dot product satisfies the following properties:
Commutative: \vec {a}\cdot \vec {b} = \vec {b}\cdot \vec {a}
Distributive: \vec {a}\cdot (\vec {b} + \vec {c}) = \vec {a}\cdot \vec {b} + \vec {a}\cdot \vec {c}
Bilinear: \vec {a}\cdot (k\vec {b}) = k(\vec {a}\cdot \vec {b}) = (\vec {a}\cdot k\vec {b})
Scalar Multiplication: (c_1\vec {a}) \cdot (c_2\vec {b}) = c_1c_2(\vec {a}\cdot \vec {b})
Orthogonality: If \vec {a}\cdot \vec {b} = 0, then \vec {a} and \vec {b} are orthogonal
Product Rule: If \vec {a} and \vec {b} are vector valued differentiable functions then the derivative of \vec {a}\cdot \vec {b} is given by the rule (\vec {a}\cdot \vec {b})' = \vec {a}'\cdot \vec {b} + \vec {a}\cdot \vec {b}'

In Euclidean space, a Euclidean vector is a geometric object that possesses both a norm and a direction. The dot product of two vectors \vec {a} and \vec {b} is defined as
\vec {a}\cdot \vec {b} = \lVert \vec {a}\rVert \lVert \vec {b}\rVert \cos \theta
where \theta is the angle between the two vectors.

Two points determine a line, and so does a point and a vector. Define the base point vector \vec {b}=(x,y,z) and the direction vector \vec {v}=(a,b,c) then the line is given by \vec {r}(t)
\vec {r}(t) = t\vec {v} + \vec {b} = (at+x, bt+y, ct+z)
Solving for t in the equation we get
t = \frac {x-at}{a} = \frac {y-bt}{b} = \frac {z-ct}{c}
which is the equation of line.

The determinant has various properties and applications in linear algebra and geometry. For us the most useful thing about it will be how it relates to volume: the determinant of a matrix gives the signed volume of the parallelepiped that is generated by the vectors given by the matrix columns.

Determinants can be introduced in a variety of different ways but many of them are not at all clear. It usually relates to volume hence we will actually use our intuitive understanding of volumes and three properties that we expected volume to have to derive the determinant (It is uniquely determined!).

So how do we expect volume to behave? First we expect a unit cube to have a volume of one. Second we expect the degenerate parallelepiped to have a volume of zero. Basically in n dimensions any n-1 dimensions object has zero n-D volume. Third we expect that volumes to be linear. Now with these three properties we move to the actual mathematics.

Suppose we have a parallelepiped \mathscr {P}\in \mathbb {R}^n whose edges are given by v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_n\in \mathbb {R}^n. We sat that the parallelepiped \mathscr {P} is the span of the vectors v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_n and write \mathscr {P}=\text {span}\{v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_n\} (Note that this span is different from linear span). We want to find function D:\mathbb {R}^{n\times n}\to \mathbb {R} which takes v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_n or a matrix with v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_n as columns to a real number which is the volume of \mathscr {P}. Now we present the three properties in mathematical form.

html:ul.html:li: D(I) = I where I = [e_1, e_2, \cdots , e_n] is the identity matrix.
D(v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_n) = 0 if v_i = v_j for any i\neq j.

D(v_1, \cdots , v_{j-1}, v+cw, v_{j+1}, \cdots , v_n) \\ = D(v_1, \cdots , v_{j-1}, v, v_{j+1}, \cdots , v_n) + cD(v_1, \cdots , v_{j-1}, w, v_{j+1}, \cdots , v_n) for any 1 \leq j \leq n, that is, D is linear.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Now we use these properties of volume to derive several other useful properties. The first property is that the volumes are signed.

html:ul.html:li:
D is alternating, if we switch any two vectors the sign changes.
D(v_1, \cdots , v_i, \cdots , v_j, \cdots , v_n) = -D(v_1, \cdots , v_j, \cdots , v_i, \cdots , v_n)

If v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_n are linear dependent then
D(v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_n) = 0
Adding a multiple of one vector to another does not change the determinant.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We almost ready to derive the formula for determinant. The final ingredient we need to do is permutations.

A permutation of a set S is a bijection from S to itself. The set of permutation of \{1,\cdots , n\} is usually denoted by S_n. We often denote a particular permutation \sigma by Cauchy's two-line notation:
\begin {bmatrix} 1 & 2 & \cdots & n \\ \sigma (1) & \sigma (2) & \cdots & \sigma (n) \end {bmatrix}
or Cauchy's one-line notation: (\sigma (1),\sigma (2),\cdots ,\sigma (n)). Another common notation is the cycle notation:
(i_1\ i_2\ \cdots \ i_k) which means i_1 \to i_2 \to \cdots \to i_k \to i_1.
A permutation in which only two elements are exchanged is called a transposition. The notation is \tau _{i,j} where i and j are the two elements exchanged while the others remain fixed.

Notice that the composition of two permutations is also a permutation. And for any permutation \sigma we can perform a series of transpositions to get the identity permutation. It turns out that the count of the number of transpositions needed to get the identity permutation is always the same, which is called the parity of the permutation.

The sign of a permutation \sigma \in S_n is a function \text {sgn}:S_n\to \{-1,1\} defined as \text {sgn}(\sigma ) = 1 if \sigma requires an even number of permutations and \text {sgn}(\sigma ) = -1 if \sigma requires an odd number of permutations to get the identity permutation.

It's easy to validate that the following properties of the determinant holds:
D(AB) = D(A)D(B)
D(A) = D(A^T) The second statement for transpose of A indicates that all the properties above also holds for row as well.

Since f'(x_0) represents the slope of the line tangent to the graph of f at (x_0, f(x_0)), differentiability of f at x_0 means that there exists a number m st
\lim _{x\to x_0} \frac {|f(x) - f(x_0) - m(x-x_0)|}{|x-x_0|} = 0
Now consider the function T:\mathbb {R}\to \mathbb {R} where T(s) = ms
T(s+t) = m(s+t) = ms + mt = T(s) + T(t) \\ T(cs) = mcs = c(ms) = cT(s)
then T is a linear transformation. In fact T is the linear function that most closely approximates the function f at the point (x_0, f(x_0)). So for x values that are very close to x_0 we have
f(x) \approx m(x-x_0) + f(x_0)

Now let's generalize the concept of derivatives to functions of the form f:\mathbb {R}^n\to \mathbb {R}^m. We assume the function f has the form
\begin {align*} &f(x_1, x_2, \cdots , x_n) = \\ &(f_1(x_1, x_2, \cdots , x_n), f_2(x_1, x_2, \cdots , x_n), \cdots , f_m(x_1, x_2, \cdots , x_n)) \end {align*}
We want to search for this linear transformation which we will denoted by Df, that most closely approximates this function f:\mathbb {R}^n\to \mathbb {R}^m at some specific point x_0=(x_{1_0}, x_{2_0}, \cdots , x_{n_0}) \in \mathbb {R}^n. If f is differentiable at x_0 then there exists a linear transformation Df(x_0):\mathbb {R}^n\to \mathbb {R}^m such that
\lim _{x\to x_0} \frac { \lVert f(x) - f(x_0) - Df(x_0)(x-x_0) \rVert }{\lVert x-x_0\rVert } = 0
The \lVert \cdot \rVert represents the Euclidean norm of the vector (Multi-dimensional version of the absolute value)
\lVert \vec {x}\rVert = \sqrt {x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2} = \sqrt {\sum _{i=1}^n x_i^2}
which is just the length of the vector. This allows us to perform dividing.
